title: This, that, and the things around you
goal: Point at things, ask what they're called, and say whether something is there or not — while learning that Javanese has three words for "this/that" but krama needs only one.
bekal: tell *iki*, *kuwi* and *kaé* apart by distance from the speaker
ask *apa iki?* and answer with the name of the thing
use *ana* / *ora ana* to say something is or isn't there

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Rini nuduhaké kamar
dialogs.intro: Rini shows Dian around the boarding house: her room, the bathroom, the shared kitchen. She speaks ngoko because they're the same age.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Iki kamarmu. Rada cilik, nanging resik.
lines.id: This is your room. It's a bit small, but clean.
lines.literal: this room-your. rather small, but clean.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Kuwi lemari. Lawang lemariné rada seret.
lines.id: That's the wardrobe. Its door sticks a bit.
lines.literal: that wardrobe. door wardrobe-the rather stiff.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Ana. Iki kunci kamar, kuwi kunci lemari.
lines.id: Yes. This is the room key, that's the wardrobe key.
lines.literal: there-is. this key room, that key wardrobe.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Kaé, sing cèt biru. Banyuné akèh, aja kuwatir.
lines.id: Over there, the one painted blue. There's plenty of water, don't worry.
lines.literal: that-over-there, which paint blue. water-the much, don't worry.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Ora. Pawon ing ngisor. Ing ndhuwur ora ana pawon.
lines.id: No. The kitchen is downstairs. There's no kitchen upstairs.
lines.literal: no. kitchen at below. at above not there-is kitchen.

notes: **Rada** means "rather, a bit": *rada cilik* (a bit small), *rada adoh* (rather far), *rada larang* (a bit expensive). Its krama form is *radi*.
**Ora apa-apa** — literally "not what-what": "it's nothing, no problem". The krama form is *boten punapa-punapa*, which is very long and so is often shortened to *boten napa-napa*.

**Lemariné** = *lemari* + *-né*. The ending *-é* / *-né* can mean "his/her" (*lemariné Rini*, Rini's wardrobe) or simply "the one we're talking about" ("the wardrobe"). The rule is simple: words ending in a consonant take **-é** (*lawang* → *lawangé*), words ending in a vowel take **-né** (*lemari* → *lemariné*).

**Ana kunciné?** — to ask "is there…?", Javanese needs no question word at all. Just raise your voice at the end, as you can in English ("There's a key?"). To be clearer, put *apa* in front: *apa ana kunciné?*

**Sing cèt biru** — *sing* means "the one that, which", and it's used constantly for pointing things out: *sing gedhé* (the big one), *sing kuwi* (that one), *sing anyar* (the new one). Its krama form is *ingkang*, often shortened to *kang*.

**Aja** is "don't", and it's only for telling people not to do something. Ordinary statements are negated with *ora*. Compare: *aja lunga* (don't go) with *ora lunga* (not going). The krama form of *aja* is *sampun* — and yes, it's exactly the same word as *sampun* "already". Tone and position tell them apart.
**Ngono** means "like that", sibling of *ngéné* (like this) and *ngana* (like that, further away). *Oh, ngono* is the most common reply when someone has just understood something — "oh, I see".

grammars.title: Three distances in ngoko, one in krama
body: Javanese splits "this/that" into three by distance — like old English "this / that / yon" — where modern English has only two.
after: Look at the fourth column: **krama flattens all three into *menika***. Good news — in polite conversation you need only one word. *Punika* is also used and means the same; *menika* is heard more in Yogyakarta and Solo.

Short forms are very common in fast speech: *kuwi* is often just **kuwi** or **ki** depending on the region, and *iki* is often said as just **ki** — *ki apa?* for "what's this?". You'll hear it a lot; no need to copy it yet.
Pointing words can also follow a noun: *buku iki* (book this = this book), *omah kuwi* (that house), *gunung kaé* (that mountain over there).

grammars.title: Ana and ora ana
body: To say something is or isn't there, Javanese uses a single word — *ana*, "there is".

head: English
Ngoko
Krama
rows: There's a wardrobe in the room.

after: **Ana** also means "to be (somewhere)": *Rini ana ing kamar* (Rini is in the room). One word, two jobs.
To negate a **noun** — "it's not X" — use **dudu**, not *ora*: *iki dudu kunciku* (this isn't my key). *Ora* negates verbs and adjectives; *dudu* negates nouns. The krama form of *dudu* is *sanès*.

sections.title: Things in your room and around the house

blocks.text: This unit's words were chosen from things that are really around you right now. Read the table while pointing at each object — two rounds are usually enough to make them stick.

Count the rows with **–** in the krama column. Fourteen of the sixteen words in this table are **the same** in ngoko and krama. That's what undha-usuk really looks like: not two complete vocabularies, but one vocabulary in which about two hundred words split in two.
Position words in Javanese are almost always preceded by *ing* or *nang* ("at, in"), then the direction word: *ing ndhuwur méja* = at top table = on the table.

head: Ngoko
Krama
English
Example
rows: *ing ngarep kos* — in front of the boarding house
*ing kiwa lawang* — left of the door
*ing tengen lemari* — right of the wardrobe
*ing tengah kamar* — in the middle of the room

blocks.text: **Ing** and **nang** both mean "at, in" and are interchangeable. *Ing* is a little neater and more common in writing; *nang* is more casual and more common in speech. There's also *ana ing* for emphasis. The krama form is *wonten ing*, often shortened to *wonten*.

blocks.title: A small trap: ndhuwur and ngisor
items: Both start with a cluster: *ndhuwur* has **n + dh**, not plain *d*; *ngisor* starts with **ng**, the sound at the end of *sing*, not a plain *n*. Words starting with *ng* and *ny* are perfectly normal in Javanese, even if they feel strange to an English tongue.
The base words are *dhuwur* (high) and *isor*, and the prefix *n-* / *ng-* turns them into place words. You'll meet this prefix again in Unit 8, where it does a much bigger job.

exercises.prompt: Answer with *ana* or *ora ana*, then write the krama form too.

items: There are clothes in the wardrobe.
There's plenty of water, don't worry.
The book is on the table.
